title: Purim: Esther
hookLine: a queen, a villain and a hidden God whose name never appears in the book

lines: A KING, A QUEEN, A SECRET.
A PLOT, AND LOTS CAST FOR A DAY.
cards: Here's a story with everything. A king of Persia who throws a party for half a year. A queen who refuses his summons and is sent away.
A beauty contest across the empire, won by a young Jewish woman who keeps her background secret, on her cousin's advice.
A proud official who demands everyone bow to him, and when one Jew won't, plots to wipe out every Jew in the kingdom, and casts lots to pick the day. A sleepless king, a banquet, a sudden reversal.
It reads like a palace thriller. And in the whole book, one name never appears.

teach.b: The book is Esther, and on Purim it's read aloud from a handwritten scroll called the megillah. Megillah just means scroll, from a root meaning to roll.
Purim means lots, the lots Haman cast to choose the day of destruction.
And the name that never appears is God's. Not once. No miracles, no prophets, no voice from heaven.

teach.h: FOR SUCH A TIME AS THIS.
teach.b: There's a queen who has to decide whether to risk her life by walking in to the king uninvited, and a cousin, Mordecai, who tells her that if she stays silent, help will come from somewhere else, and adds: "who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?"
She goes in. Everything turns. The Talmud plays on this.

It hears in the name Esther the Hebrew for hidden, and links her to a verse in Deuteronomy where God says: "And I will surely hide My face in that day." So the book of Esther becomes the story of a hidden God.

Not absent, hidden. Working through coincidences, a king's insomnia, a brave woman's choice. Some readers find ordinary life in this: no parted seas, just timing and courage, and, looking back, a pattern.
One reason people give for Purim's costumes and masks: they hide who's underneath, the way God is hidden in the story.
And look at this week: a hut of branches, four kinds bound together, dancing with the scrolls, lights in the window, a count going up, a tree's birthday, and now a hidden name.

how: On Purim, Jews hear the book of Esther read aloud from a handwritten scroll, the megillah, both in the evening and again the next morning, often in costume.

games.q: you're Esther. going to the king uninvited could cost your life. Mordecai says your people are in danger. what do you do?
o: stay silent; help will come some other way.
go in to the king uninvited.
games.why: she asks the Jews to fast for three days, then goes in: 'if I perish, I perish.' the king holds out his scepter, and the story turns.

practice: Think back over the last year to a moment when something turned out right and at the time just looked like luck: a call at the right moment, a stranger, a delay that saved you.
Replay it slowly; you don't have to decide what it was, just notice that it was there.

wordCard.voice: Megillah. A scroll, and on Purim, the scroll of Esther, read aloud: a story where God's name never appears.

carryVoice: Your line: hidden, not absent. Help doesn't always announce itself. One hundred thirty-three days in.
